records.title: Record June 2023 marine heatwave across the North Sea and northwest European shelf
records.description: A Met Office-led study found the northwest European shelf average ran 2.9 C above the June norm for 16 days, its longest recorded category II marine heatwave, with local anomalies up to 5 C in the central North Sea. A University of Exeter, Met Office and Cefas study reports that the event disrupted phytoplankton blooms and that the annual chance of such an event in the central North Sea rose from 0.7% to 9.8% between 1993 and recent years.

location.name: North Sea and northwest European shelf
location.detail: Shelf-wide event around the UK and Ireland; peak week 19-26 June 2023 with local +5 C anomalies in the central and western North Sea (ref 3).

records.layer_rationale: Physical ocean warming event driven by high pressure and long-term shelf warming.

notes.harm: Exeter reports the event significantly disrupted phytoplankton blooms, but its full effect on the ecosystem is still being assessed (ref 1); no mortality is documented, so potential or limited harm.
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources reports a fishery closure or other restriction tied to the June 2023 event (refs 1-3).
notes.scale: The shelf-wide average, including the North Sea, was +2.9 C above the June climatology (ref 3), a regional-sea event.
notes.duration: The shelf average stayed in category II for 16 days (ref 3), days to weeks.
notes.significance: NOAA declared a category IV marine heatwave for parts of the shelf on 17 June 2023 (ref 3) and the Met Office led the peer-reviewed analysis (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The shelf average underwent its longest recorded category II marine heatwave, 16 days at +2.9 C above the June average, with local anomalies up to +5 C (ref 3).

records.title: North Sea sets record spring, summer and annual temperatures in 2025 and runs hot again in 2026
records.description: The German Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) reported the warmest North Sea spring (8.7 C), summer (15.7 C) and year (11.6 C) since its series began, with every month of 2025 above the long-term average. BSH says marine heatwaves are becoming longer and more frequent, and a September 2026 BSH-based report counts 66 marine heatwave days at its Helgoland station by early September 2026.

location.name: North Sea (German Bight to Norway and the Channel)
location.detail: BSH basin-wide analysis; largest anomalies off Norway and Denmark in spring, and in the western and southwestern North Sea up to the English Channel in summer (refs 1, 2).

records.layer_rationale: Record basin-wide sea temperatures are a physical climate signal.

notes.harm: BSH says marine heatwaves add pressure on marine ecosystems (ref 3) and NOC observed intense southern North Sea blooms in May 2025 (ref 5), but no mortality is documented, so potential harm.
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources reports a fishery or tourism restriction from the 2025 North Sea warmth (refs 1-5).
notes.scale: The BSH records cover the whole North Sea, a regional sea (refs 1-3).
notes.duration: Every month of 2025 was above the long-term average and the annual mean set a record (ref 3); a further heatwave is counted in 2026 (ref 4).
notes.significance: BSH, the German national agency, formally reported the records and the 11.6 C annual mean as the warmest since 1969 (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: North Sea annual surface temperature 11.6 C in 2025, the warmest since BSH measurements began in 1969, with June and December setting monthly records (ref 3).

measures.note: 0.9 C above the long-term average, warmest since analyses began in 1997 (ref 1).

records.title: Skagerrak marine heatwave in July 2025 equals the temperature record while kelp retreats along the coast
records.description: The Norwegian Meteorological Institute reported sea temperatures of 22-23 C, at least 5 C above normal, from Trondelag to Sweden and Denmark in July 2025. The Institute of Marine Research recorded 23.8 C at its Skagerrak station on 24 July, matching the 2008 record, while the Norwegian Environment Agency reported in October 2025 that kelp and large algae now grow at least 3 m shallower at over 40% of monitored Skagerrak stations.

notes.harm: Okokyst monitoring found kelp and large algae growing at least 3 m shallower at over 40% of Skagerrak stations and algal condition worse in 60% of areas (ref 2); heat is one of several drivers named.
notes.livelihoods: No fishery or aquaculture restriction on the Skagerrak coast is reported; only a warning of stress to fish and a 2024 lice surge in northern Norway (ref 1).
notes.scale: The warm water ran from the Trondelag coast to Sweden and Denmark (ref 1) and the kelp decline spans the Skagerrak coast (ref 2), a regional sea.
notes.duration: The algae decline covers 2021-2024 (ref 2) and the heat event came in summer 2025 (ref 1), so recurring over years.
notes.significance: The Norwegian Environment Agency published the monitoring finding as a formal agency report and plans a 2025-summer impact analysis (ref 2).

records.title: Hemsby cliff-top homes demolished as erosion takes half of a 30-year forecast in one winter
records.description: Great Yarmouth Borough Council warned owners of 14 homes on The Marrams and Fakes Road in January 2026 that they could collapse onto the beach and advised residents to vacate. An April 2026 report says 32 properties had been demolished at Hemsby since December and roughly half of the erosion predicted for the next 30 years happened over the winter.

records.title: German Wadden Sea tidal basins found no longer to keep pace with sea level rise

records.title: UK sandeel fishing closure in the North Sea upheld in Scottish waters and partly in English waters by EU-UK arbitration
records.description: On 26 March 2024 Scotland closed all its waters to sandeel fishing and the UK closed English North Sea waters through a licence condition. The EU challenged both closures under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. An arbitration tribunal ruling published on 2 May 2025 upheld the Scottish closure fully and found a procedural failure on proportionality in the English one; the UK says a new decision process completed in June 2025 resolves it and the closures remain. A three-member Permanent Court of Arbitration tribunal ruled in May 2025 that the UK's full closure of sandeel fishing in English waters breached the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement because it was not proportionate for EU vessels, but rejected the EU's other three claims, including on the Scottish closure and on scientific evidence. The UK said it was not legally obliged to reverse the closure of English waters. Danish industry says the ban costs it about 40 million pounds a year.

records.description: On 10 March 2025 the container ship Solong collided with the anchored tanker Stena Immaculate, which carried 220,204.5 barrels of aviation fuel, 14 nautical miles north-east of Spurn Head. The Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) interim report says the collision breached the No.7 port cargo tank, the escaping fuel ignited and the fire spread to containers on Solong; 36 crew were recovered and one Solong crew member is presumed dead. The volume of fuel that reached the sea is not stated in the interim report, and the MAIB investigation was still listed as current on 2 October 2026. On 10 March 2025 the container ship Solong, making about 16 knots, struck the anchored tanker Stena Immaculate about 14 nautical miles north-east of Spurn Head, breaching a cargo tank and igniting aviation fuel and containers. The UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch's April 2025 interim report found neither ship had a dedicated lookout and that one Solong crew member is missing, presumed dead. records.title: Record hydrogen sulphide and a third of the Baltic Proper seabed hypoxic, 2023 to 2026
records.description: SMHI's preliminary figures show anoxia on about 18 percent and hypoxia on about 34 percent of Baltic bottom areas in 2024, with hydrogen sulphide at the highest levels ever recorded in the East Gotland Basin. SMHI research cruises in July and August 2025 and July 2026 still found hydrogen sulphide from 70 to 125 m and acute oxygen shortage from 60 to 90 m in the Gotland basins. A peer-reviewed study describes the 2016 to 2024 stagnation as unprecedented deoxygenation. SMHI's oxygen survey for 2024 found anoxia on about 18% and hypoxia (including anoxia) on about 34% of Baltic Sea bottom area, with hydrogen sulphide at record levels in all basins around Gotland. The agency says the severe conditions have persisted since a 1999 regime shift and that inflows have been too small to change the overall picture.

records.title: Round goby now established along most of the Baltic coast and is reshaping Swedish coastal fish communities
records.description: The non-native round goby, first recorded in the Gulf of Gdansk in 1990 and in Sweden's Karlskrona archipelago in 2008, now occupies most of the Baltic coastline and has reached Ornskoldsvik in the north. records.title: Disabled crude tanker Eventin with about 100,000 tonnes of oil held off Rügen since January 2025
records.description: The nearly 20-year-old Panama-flagged tanker Eventin lost power on 9 January 2025 with about 100,000 tonnes of Russian crude aboard and drifted into German waters before being towed to an anchorage off Sassnitz on Rügen. The tanker Eventin lost power in the Baltic on 9 January 2025 and drifted into German territorial waters, and was towed to an anchorage near Sassnitz on Rügen where it remains detained. records.title: Bornholm Energy Island: 3 GW Baltic offshore wind hub paused in 2025, permitted in 2026 with completion not before 2034
records.description: Bornholm Energy Island is planned to bundle about 3 GW from three offshore wind farms and send power by about 370 km of subsea cable to Denmark and Germany. Denmark put it on hold in early 2025, Energinet received environmental permits on 30 January 2026, and Germany and Denmark agreed a cost split in early 2026. Commissioning is expected in 2034 according to 50Hertz, while a Danish trade report captions 2036.

records.title: HELCOM meetings with Russia suspended since March 2022 under a strategic pause
records.description: Since 4 March 2022 the EU and HELCOM's EU member states have suspended official HELCOM meetings and projects involving Russia, which remains one of ten Contracting Parties to the Helsinki Convention. The "H9" group reaffirmed the strategic pause at the 2024 ministerial meeting and HELCOM work continues without Russia. The European Commission noted in April 2024 that the third HELCOM state report found little improvement between 2016 and 2021.

location.name: HELCOM / Helsinki Convention area
location.detail: Baltic Sea regional environmental governance body with its secretariat in Helsinki.

records.layer_rationale: A regional sea convention operating without one of its Baltic coastal parties.

notes.harm: The European Commission said the third HELCOM state report found little improvement between 2016 and 2021 and that the Baltic is in a bad environmental state (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited pages describe no closures or restrictions; HELCOM estimates the sea's condition costs about EUR 5.6 billion a year (ref 2).
notes.scale: The pause affects Baltic-wide cooperation under the Helsinki Convention (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Meetings with Russia have been suspended since 4 March 2022 and "until further notice" per HELCOM (ref 1).
notes.significance: The German chairmanship suspended HELCOM meetings involving Russia and the Contracting Parties reaffirmed the strategic pause at the 2024 ministerial meeting (ref 1).
